newsitem.title: PERU: Peru, rebels restart talks, but no agreement yet.
newsitem.headline: Peru, rebels restart talks, but no agreement yet.

text.p: The Peruvian government and Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home restarted their troubled negotiation process Wednesday in a bid to resolve the 85-day crisis peacefully.
But the 10th round of talks -- between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa -- brought no sign of agreement.

A statement from a three-member committee overseeing the taks noted that the meeting was held with "the same cordiality" as previous ones and had involved mutual discussion of each side's initial positions.

"With there not being agreements on some matters, a stage of reflection is necessary, in which the guarantors' commission and the observer will seek to facilitate through separate meetings alternatives that make a solution viable," said the statement read by Peruvian Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, the Vatican's representative on the committee.
He added that the committee, which also includes Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent and Red Cross chief representative Michel Minnig, would soon announce the date of an 11th round of talks.
Earlier, a white Red Cross car drove Cerpa and his second- in-command Rolly Rojas across the street from the residence to a safe house where nine previous rounds of talks were held.

As the Red Cross car pulled out of the compound, the 20-odd hostage-takers who remained at the residence sang their rebel hymn in honour of MRTA members killed in fighting with Peru's security forces.
As well as Palermo and the guarantors, Japanese government observer, Terusuke Terada, was also present.
The first face-to-face dialogue in a week was possible after the guarantors commission held meetings over the last two days with Cerpa and Palermo to coax the two sides back to the negotiating table.
Until last week, the talks to end the siege peacefully seemed to be progressing steadily.
But last Thursday the rebels refused to attend talks, charging the government with planning to take the building by storm through a secret tunnel.

After energetic meetings with both sides, the guarantors arranged for a fresh round of talks on Monday, only to have the government abruptly call off that meeting, accusing the rebels of trying to backtrack on the progress already made.
Before Wednesday's talks, President Alberto Fujimori continued his propaganda trail around traditionally strong rebel areas in the Amazon jungle to win the hearts and minds of peasants.

"Even in this part of the jungle, so far from the capital, people want peace. They do not want violence. They do not want these movements calling themselves revolutionaries," Fujimori told the villagers of Papaplaya in the Huallaga valley 600 miles (960 km) to the north of Lima.

On the second day of a tour to the northern jungle, the president followed his inauguration of government-financed works Tuesday by handing out clothes and blankets to peasants left homeless from recent flash-floods around the region.

The United Nations Human Rights Commission also had harsh words for the MRTA on Wednesday. In a statement issued from Geneva, the commission condemned the rebels as "terrorist elements" and said hostage-taking anywhere violated human rights.

The siege began Dec. 17 when the rebels invaded a cocktail party hosted by the Japanese ambassador and took all the guests hostage. The rebels released most of them in the first few days, but kept some as bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother, Pedro, two of his cabinet ministers, the Japanese ambassador and a long list of Japanese businessmen.

The 72 men held by the MRTA, who are demanding freedom for about 400 jailed comrades, are basically in good health but are showing growing signs of chronic stress, including gum disease and skin ailments, after 85 days in captivity, said a doctor who is accompanying a Red Cross team treating them.
